source.title: Details or Artifacts: A Locally Discriminative Learning Approach to Realistic Image Super-Resolution
source.role_reason: 引言以图1区分平滑区域、随机纹理和细结构三类图像块，解释GAN超分辨率在C类出现不自然伪影的失败机制；并非一般结果拼图。
source.caption:
Figure 1. Three representative types of SISR regions generated by
ESRGAN [40]. For each example, the left is an LR patch and the
right is its GAN-SR result. Type A patches represent regions that
are easy to super-resolve, e.g., smooth and large-scale structural
areas, where the main structures are preserved in the LR input. In
contrast, patches of type B and type C are with fine-scale details,
which are hard to be faithfully restored due to the signal alias-
ing in the LR inputs. The results of texture-like type B patches
are perceptually realistic despite the pixel-wise differences to the
ground-truth, since the patterns are naturally irregular with weak
priorsforobservers. However,theresultsoftypeCpatchesexhibit
perceptually unpleasant visual artifacts since the overshoot pixels
and distorted structures are sensitive to human perception.

source.title: Instance-Free Domain Adaptive Object Detection
source.role_reason: 图1及引言以野生动物采集场景说明获取目标实例成本高，而背景图易得，概念对比传统DAOD与无实例设置。
source.caption:
Figure 1. Illustration of Instance-Free DAOD. The orange time-
line indicates that target-domain instances appear only after a
long waiting period and require costly manual screening. Tradi-
tional DAOD (top) relies on target images containing foreground
instances, whereas Instance-Free DAOD (bottom) enables transfer-
ring using only background-only target images.

observations.evidence: The upper and lower comparisons distinguish training with target-domain animals from instance-free target training, while retaining the same inference example. Repeated empty frames and an hourglass convey waiting for an animal to appear.
observations.limitation: The dashed animal silhouette leaves some uncertainty about whether the lower training image represents absence or deliberate removal.

Figure 1: Three unresolved challenges in taxonomy-aware segmentation. Left: identical visual
concepts can be split, merged, or omitted by different annotation policies. Center: a coarse label such
as vehicle is compatible with several semantic atoms, but the correct relation changes with local visual
evidence, which a class name alone cannot observe. Right: forward-only supervision can preserve an
apparently correct coarse mask even when distinct atom channels become indistinguishable. A useful
compiler must therefore be local, visually grounded, and semantically recoverable.

source.caption:
Figure 3: SeSAM framework for coarse sup ervision. First, pseudo-labels for training images are
generated by the teacher model. Next, these pseudo-labels are then refined following the key steps 1-3,
namely instance separation, point sampling and mask selection (see Section 3). To improve mask quality,
we augment coarse labels with high-confidence pseudo-labels before applying SAM (step 0). The resulting
refined labels, called SeSAM labels, are then used to train the student network.

source.role_reason: 图2明确为整体方法，展示图像特征到SDF几何、反照率和阴影网络，再到完整三维输出。
source.caption:
Figure 2. Overview of our method. The feature extractor network G produces pixel-aligned features z from an input image I for all points
x
in space x. The implicit signed distance function network f computes the distance d to the closest surface given a point and its feature.
Additionally f returns albedo colors a defined for surface points. The shading network s predicts the shading for surface points given its
surface normal n , as well as illumination l. On the right we show the reconstruction of geometry and albedo colors, and the shaded 3D
x
geometry.

source.caption:
Figure 1. Attention visualization at selected query points. We
show an input resized to 512 × 512 using the CLIP ViT-B/16 vi-
sion encoder. For each colored query, we compare the attention
maps produced by CLIP [51], NACLIP [26], and our PEARL.
CLIP exhibits diffuse and background-biased responses, while
NACLIP improves localization but often fragments objects into
isolated peaks. By performing Procrustes alignment in the last
self-attention block, PEARL yields compact and object-consistent
attention, suppresses background spill, and better preserves thin
parts, resulting in stable focus with reduced grid artifacts.

Figure 1. The concat and frame-by-frame operations in exist-
ing methods struggle to efficiently extract sub-pixels and suppress
noise, leading to remaining artifacts and over-smoothed details, as
shown in (a). We observe that noise randomly appears on several
frames, while effective sub-pixels have consistent intensity at cor-
responding positions in all frames, as shown in (c). Based on this,
a novel inter-frame query and intra-frame scanning-based QMam-
baBSR is proposed to extract more accurate sub-pixels while mit-
igating noise interference simultaneously, as shown in (b).

source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of TOCOMAS. Task-derived responsibility regions organize agents, handoffs,
and memory boundaries; online evolution preserves their coherence.

observations.evidence: Three upper modules identify task organization, agent collaboration, and memory coordination. The lower sequence shows feedback, structural proposals, screening, evaluation, and an accepted-organization loop.
observations.limitation: The handoff gate's connection to agent exchanges and the operational meaning of the arrows between upper modules remain unclear.

observations.evidence: The three upper modules show task organization, agent orchestration, and memory coordination; the lower pipeline shows structural proposals, screening, and acceptance.
observations.limitation: The upper modules' operational sequence and the attachment of floating evidence/context labels to particular handoffs remain partly unclear.

source.role_reason: 图注与第4节说明从真实相机成像到NeRF、体渲染、RGB/事件CRF及两路监督的完整训练流程；不是单独CRF模块图4。
source.caption:
Figure 3. The data generation process of event and RGB cameras (upper parts) and the pipeline of See-NeRF (lower parts) are shown in the
figure. We use NeRF to represent the actual radiance of an extreme lighting scene in the HDR domain. The volume rendering simulates the
raw scene radiance rays hitting the sensor and obtaining the raw sensor values. The predicted LDR images and events are generated with our
proposed sensor-physics grounded RGB and event CRF models (details are shown in the right part of the figure). The image loss and event
loss are employed to jointly supervise the optimization of the two CRF models and the NeRF network.

source.caption:
Figure 3: The pipeline of our method. Multi-view image streams are processed in a block-wise
manner. Each image block is first encoded with intrinsic priors and then processed by a spatio-
temporal decoder. By maintaining a streamed KV memory across consecutive blocks, the model
continuously extracts consistent geometry features for multi-task predictions, including ego-centric
motion and dense metric 3D reconstruction.

Figure 1. Our Carve3D algorithm steadily improves the 3D con-
sistency of a multi-view diffusion model and the resulting quality
of the NeRF and the mesh, without sacrificing its image-prompt
alignment, texture details, or realism. Here, we show 3 testing-
set results (in 3 rows, numbered as 1-3, separated by dotted lines)
from the finetuning process (epoch 0, 28, and 55 in 3 columns).
Each row includes the generated multi-view images (denoted as
MV), the reconstructed NeRF and extracted mesh (denoted as RM)
and the text prompt (denoted as TP). The inconsistencies in the
multi-view images, e.g. the facing direction of the shopping cart,
the position of the octopus arms, and the position of the pencils,
lead to artifacts in the NeRF and the mesh (highlighted in red).

source.title: When Should AI Chime In?  Benchmarking Timely Contribution of Proactive Agents in Multi-Party Chat
source.role_reason: 图1及引言说明四阶段数据收集协议和三种模型评测设置，属于整体研究流程。
source.caption:
Figure 1: PITCH (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat) is the first benchmark for proactive inter-
vention timing built from unscripted human conversations and participants’ own judgments of when
proactive interjections should occur. We collected the benchmark data via a four-phrase protocol:
Conversation, Message Contribution, Timing Judgments, and Deliberation. We then evaluated 15
models across 28 configurations against the benchmark in three task setups that differ in their task
difficulty and realism for real-world deployment of agents in group conversations.

source.caption:
Figure 2. NeuralRecon architecture. NeuralRecon predicts TSDF with a three-level coarse-to-fine approach that gradually increases the
density of sparse voxels. Key-frame images in the local fragment are first passed through the image backbone to extract the multi-level
features. These image features are later back-projected along each ray and aggregated into a 3D feature volume Fl, where l represents the
t
level index. At the first level (l = 1), a dense TSDF volume S1 is predicted. At the second and third levels, the upsampled Sl−1 from the
t t
last level is concatenated with Fl and used as the input for the GRU Fusion and MLP modules. A feature volume defined in the world
t
frame is maintained at each level as the global hidden state of the GRU. At the last level, the output Sl is used to replace corresponding
t
voxels in the global TSDF volume Sg, yielding the final reconstruction at time t.

source.title: LLMDet: Learning Strong Open-Vocabulary Object Detectors under the Supervision of Large Language Models
source.role_reason: 图4及第4节明确展示LLMDet总体架构，包含检测器、图像级和区域级LLM分支以及两个训练目标。
source.caption:
Figure 4. The overview of LLMDet. LLMDet contains a standard open-vocabulary detector and a large language model (LLM) and is
trained under both grounding loss and language modeling loss. The LLM is designed to generate both image-level captions using feature
maps as visual input and region-level captions using a single object query as visual input, which are separated by different prompts.
Only vision tokens in region-level generation pass through the cross-attention (CA) modules in LLM, which is highlighted by a dashed
boundary. Since the number of tokens in image-level and region-level generation varies greatly, we forward the LLM twice separately to
save memory and computation. The LLM can be discarded in the inference time so that there is no extra cost.

source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of CVRoute. (a) Street-view semantics are routed to satellite-defined regions
for satellite-space prediction. (b) Cross-view entities are matched over multiple pose hypotheses and
fused through pose-marginalized nullable routing. (c) A training-only privileged relationship teacher
guides early routing and is gradually annealed out; inference uses only predicted relationships.

source.caption:
Figure 2. Architecture of PaCo. Starting from an incomplete point cloud, we hierarchically encode the points into plane proxies with a
lookup table from segmentation. These proxies inform the proxy generator in producing a set of proxy proposals. The generated proxies
are then passed to the parameter estimator and the point distributor for primitive estimation. Finally, the primitive selector identifies a
subset of primitives to form the parametric completion, with selection optimized via bipartite matching. The resulting primitives enable
direct assembly for polygonal surface reconstruction. Points are colored according to their planar primitives.

source.title: GRASP: Grounded Restoration with Agent-Refined Semantic Prompts for Real-World Image Super-Resolution
source.role_reason: 方法节图2明确给出GRASP整体条件通路、DiT骨干和输出。
source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of GRASP. Real-ISR is cast as visual in-context completion. Local visual
evidence comes from the diptych, global image context from the Vision-Context Bridge over CLIP,
and semantic prompts from LLaVA captions during training and agent refinement during inference.

observations.evidence: Three labeled conditioning streams feed a DiT backbone, followed by a VAE decoder and image output. The bridge inset exposes its main operations.
observations.limitation: The lower-right reasoning loop does not clearly show how its generated prompts return to the backbone or text encoder.

observations.evidence: Three numbered input branches converge on the DiT backbone, followed by a VAE decoder and output image. The bridge inset explicitly shows its operation sequence.
observations.limitation: The refinement loop does not clearly show how the agent's generated text re-enters the model; its arrows connect back toward the output image.

source.role_reason: 第3.2节Overview及图2将视觉语言特征、归一化、分布差异、联合双边上采样及输出串成完整推理链路，是总体框架。
source.caption:
Figure 2. Overview of the proposed method. The pipeline begins by computing the cosine similarity (Cos.) between vision-language
features to obtain logits, followed by non-maximum suppression (NMS) and normalization (Norm.) to filter low-confidence patches. The
core step involves calculating the distribution discrepancy between the normalized logits and the degenerate distribution map. This solved
discrepancy is then upsampled to the original image resolution via joint bilateral upsampling (JBU) to obtain the discrepancy map. Finally,
the semantic map is generated by applying an argmax operation to the discrepancy map.

source.caption:
Figure 1. Events corresponding to a blurry LDR image contain
spatial difference (High Dynamic Range) and temporal difference
(High Temporal Resolution) information of the scene radiance,
making it an ideal data for enhancing HDR sharp 3D scene recon-
struction. See-NeRF models the physical imaging process with
proposed RGB and event CRF models to bridge the sensor-physics
discrepancy, leveraging events to infer scene dynamics and achiev-
ing sharper and better HDR novel view synthesis results compared
to the physical unaligned method EvHDR-NeRF [5].

source.role_reason: 第3.2节和图2给出从代理重建、跨视图梯度、扰动生成到目标三维重建系统的整体计算路径。
source.caption: Figure 2. Framework of PoInit-of-View.

observations.evidence: The left-to-right sequence connects clean views, a proxy pipeline, gradient-guided PGD, poisoned views, and a victim pipeline producing degraded renderings.
observations.limitation: The iterative relationship between updated views and the proxy is implicit, as is the connection from the victim pipeline to its output.

observations.evidence: The left-to-right progression connects clean views, a proxy pipeline, gradient-driven PGD, poisoned views, and a victim pipeline with a degraded rendering.
observations.limitation: The victim's internal processing sequence and connection to the rendered output are implied by placement rather than explicitly connected.

observations.evidence: The left-to-right sequence connects clean views, a proxy pipeline, gradient-driven PGD, poisoned views, and a victim pipeline producing poor-quality renderings.
observations.limitation: PGD's image input and the connection from the victim pipeline to the rendered output are implicit.

observations.evidence: Separate view frames and nested victim-pipeline boxes establish the main groups and reading order.
observations.limitation: Rotated labels inside the victim pipeline require extra reading effort, while the gradient loop and update annotations crowd the center.

observations.evidence: Outer containers separate the view sets and victim pipeline, while nested boxes group the front-end SfM operations.
observations.limitation: Numerous vertical labels inside the victim pipeline require rotated reading, and the gradient-loop region packs several annotations closely together.

observations.evidence: Nested boxes distinguish the victim pipeline and its front-end initialization stages, while the overall horizontal layout establishes reading order.
observations.limitation: Numerous rotated stage labels require extra reading effort, and the gradient loop crowds its annotation.

observations.evidence: Repeated camera symbols and view arrangements link clean and poisoned inputs. Blue connectors trace the proxy objective and gradient, while green dashed connectors trace poisoning and delivery.
observations.limitation: Explicit directional connectors give way to spatial sequencing inside the victim pipeline and before the rendered output.

observations.evidence: Repeated camera symbols and image arrangements link clean and poisoned views; blue dashed feedback and green dashed updates remain visually traceable.
observations.limitation: Green also marks victim and output headings, making its meaning broader than the perturbation encoding alone.

observations.limitation: Connector conventions become less explicit inside the victim pipeline and at its output.

source.caption:
Figure 2. Overview of our framework at incremental step t. Given an image x, the query function generates a content-aware query
representation by adaptively computing query weights via a ranking function F and performing weighted aggregation. Subsequently,
ψ
prompts are retrieved from both the shared and private pool and injected into the decoder layer. In parallel, the teacher model Φ
t−1
generates a set of candidate bounding boxes, where potentially valuable ones are projected into the feature space to compute their similarity
with class prototypes. This process yields a set of refined, high-quality pseudo-labels to guide the training of the student model Φ .
t

source.title: EAGLE: Grounding Multimodal LLM Judges for AI-Generated Image Assessment via Evidence Anchors
source.role_reason: 方法节称图2为整体框架，连接MLLM整体评分、证据分解、聚合和最终预测。
source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of EAGLE. It combines holistic MLLM scoring with anchor-guided evidence
decomposition. The decomposition branch organizes latent queries into shared and anchor-specific
groups to respectively acquire reusable evidence across judgments and cross-modal/visual evidence
anchor, followed by adaptive aggregation of these grounded judgments for criterion-specific scoring.
The decomposed prediction score is further combined with the holistic score for final assessment.

source.caption:
Figure 2. An overview of Target-perceived Dual-branch Distillation framework. To simplify the description, ROI refers to the operation
to get proposal features of each image. First, a source domain image is transferred into target-like domain. All of the images from three
domains are fed to a shared proposal extractor to get proposals and proposal features. Then, the proposal features of source and target-like
images are used to train corresponding branches with supervision of ground truth. Moreover, we feed the proposal features of a real target
domain image into both branches, for learning object knowledge from both source and target-like domains. As the images from target
domain are not annotated, the model is optimized by self-distillation.

Figure 2: Overview of the proposed approach. Given a single RGB image, our model detects object centers as key-points in a heatmap Y .
The network directly predicts shape exemplars z and 9-DoF bounding boxes jointly for all objects in the scene. The collision loss L
coll

source.caption:
Figure 3. The distributions of TP+, TP- and BG when using 10%
labeled data on COCO. ‘TP+’ means that the estimated instance
has the same class ID as the ground-truth (GT) and the IOU of
BBox is above 0.5. ‘TP-’ means that the estimated instance has
the same class ID as GT but the IOU of BBox is below 0.5. ‘BG’
means that the estimated instance belongs to the background or
has wrong class ID.

source.caption:
Figure 2. An example of GroundingCap-1M. Bounding box annotations are discarded for clarity. Compared with original short grounding
texts, the detailed captions in GroundingCap-1M are rich in object types, textures, colors, parts of the objects, object actions, precise object
locations and texts. Each caption in GroundingCap-1M has around 115 words on average.

source.caption:
Figure 1. Two typical examples of detection results on the adverse
weather conditions adaptation experiments with different methods.
Semi-supervised method UBT [27] lacks awareness of objects in
the fog. Adversarial based GPA [49] attempts to exploit the objects
in the fog but gives some wrong predictions, such as the motorcy-
cle in the first row and the person in the second row. Our methods
can predict the boxes and categories more accurately.

source.title: Beyond Background Shift: Rethinking Instance Replay in Continual Semantic Segmentation
source.role_reason: 图1及引言明确展示部分标注将旧/未来类别错当背景的问题，与实例回放概念对比；不是普通结果展示。
source.caption:
Figure 1. Comparison of traditional image replay (a) and our re-
play methods (b). (a) shows that only the old class “horse” is la-
beled in stored image, while other classes (new class “person” and
old class “car”) are labeled as background. Both old (“horse”) and
future classes in new images are labeled as background. (b) Our
method avoids confusing information in stored image by retaining
instances and alleviates background shift by fusing these instances
in the new image.

observations.evidence: The side-by-side comparison contrasts image replay with selecting and placing a stored horse instance. Orange “Background Shift” callouts and question marks visibly identify the limitation on the left.
observations.limitation: The precise meaning of background shift and why instance placement resolves it remain partly implicit.

source.caption:
Figure 2. Our PEARL framework with align-then-propagate. Given an image I and a label set Y , a frozen ViT vision encoder yields
patch tokens. Procrustes alignment is inserted in the last self-attention block: for each head (J heads), queries and keys are weighted-
centered and the keys are orthogonally rotated toward the query subspace, producing geometry-corrected patch features. A frozen text
encoder maps Y to unit-norm prototypes T . Patch-text cosine similarity gives initial logits Z(cid:101) . Text-aware Laplacian propagation then
refines Z(cid:101) on a compact grid using a class graph G induced by T and confidence weights, and the refined scores are upsampled to full
resolution F . The final segmentation S is obtained by selecting, at each pixel, the class with the highest score.

Figure 2: Network architecture. In the first stage, the network takes a single RGB image as input, and predicts a planar/non-
planar segmentation mask and pixel-level embeddings. Then, an efficient mean shift clustering algorithm is applied to

instance-level geometric consistencies.

source.caption:
Fig. 2: The proposed RefReward-SR framework. (a) MLLM Fine-tuning:
Fine-tuning via GRPO with format and LR-conditioned rank rewards from RefSR-
18K for human preference alignment. (b) Global-Local Crop Scoring: Extracting
representative local crops via RAM and Grounding DINO, then fusing multi-scale
MLLM scores via area-weighted averaging for comprehensive evaluation.

source.title: CAT: Exploiting Inter-Class Dynamics for Domain Adaptive Object Detection
source.role_reason: 图1以带颜色框的错分类与假阳性明确诊断少数类问题；引言据此引出类别偏置动机，非普通结果展示。
source.caption:
Figure 1. Performance of Class-Aware Teacher (CAT). AT [29]
(top left), with Inter-Class Loss, ICL, (top-right), with Class Rela-
tion Augmentation, CRA, (bottom-left), and CAT (bottom-right).
CAT is able to address misclassification and false positives, blue
and red boxes, respectively, in minority classes such as ’train’. The
combination of ICL and CRA further boosts performance by re-
ducing the number of false positives shown as pink boxes.

work extracts structural patterns via collaborative reasoning to generate sparsity masks and textual
priors. (2) The Structure-Aware Functional Encoder maps these patterns to attention biases in
the logit space and projects them via mask propagation. (3) The RL-Guided Alignment Module
dynamically regulates structural guidance strength Alpha (α) and alignment weight Lambda (λ).

Figure 2. Our core motivation. Based on the observations in (a) and (b), we deconstruct the complex UHD restoration problem into three
progressive stages: zero-frequency enhancement, low-frequency restoration, and high-frequency refinement.

source.title: SHAPE: Structural Hierarchy of Affinities for Patch Enhancement in Training-Free Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
source.role_reason: 图2展示SHAPE三类专家的连续完整计算过程，从图像/文本特征到边、节点、区域得分和最终分割。
source.pdf_version: ICLR 2027 frozen anonymous submission PDF; retrieved 2026-10-28 UTC
source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of SHAPE. (a) The Edge Expert uses relation-level VFM support to guide
CLIP feature aggregation. (b) The Node Expert uses a patch-specific VFM neighborhood to refine
each score. (c) The Region Expert uses an agreement-gated regional support to reduce residual
fragmentation. Together, the three experts organize VFM structure into complementary supports for
feature aggregation, patch-specific correction, and regional consistency.

source.title: Complexity Experts are Task-Discriminative Learners for Any Image Restoration
source.role_reason: 引言图1比较稠密网络、刚性MoE与复杂度专家，说明不合理参数分配和固定路由的局限。
source.caption:
Figure 1. Motivation. (a) Dense all-in-one restoration meth-
ods [24, 57] often inefficiently allocate parameters when handling
multiple degradation types. (b) While recent Mixture-of-Experts
(MoE) approaches [61, 62] address this through sparse computa-
tion, their rigid routing mechanisms uniformly distribute inputs
across experts without considering the natural relationships be-
tween degradations. (c) To overcome these limitations, we intro-
duce Complexity Experts - adaptive processing blocks with size-
varying computational units. Our framework dynamically allocates
model capacity using a spring-inspired force mechanism that con-
tinuously guides routing decisions toward simpler experts when
possible, with the force proportional to the complexity of the input
degradation. While initially designed for computational efficiency,
this approach naturally emerges as a task-discriminative learning
framework, assigning degradations to the most suitable experts.
This makes it particularly effective for all-in-one restoration meth-
ods, where both task-specific processing and cross-degradation
knowledge sharing are crucial.

source.caption:
Figure 1. (a) The synthetic images generated from Stable Diffusion and our proposed InstaGen, which can serve as a dataset synthesizer
for sourcing photo-realistic images and instance bounding boxes at scale. (b) On open-vocabulary detection, training on synthetic images
demonstrates significant improvement over CLIP-based methods on novel categories. (c) Training on the synthetic images generated from
InstaGen also enhances the detection performance in close-set scenario, particularly in data-sparse circumstances.

source.caption:
Figure 5. The architecture of the proposed DDDNet. With the input DP image pair, the DepthNet first estimates a coarse inverse depth map
Dˆ . Then, we combine the coarse and blurred inverse depth map with B , and feed them to the DeblurNet. The deblurred image and
c {L,R}
estimated inverse depth map are fed to our DP simulator to synthesize a DP image pair. The synthesized DP images are compared to the
inputs using our reblur loss (Eq. (11)), to regularise the DDDNet in training. Note that, the ground truth inverse depth maps and sharp
images are used as supervision signals in training. (Best viewed in colour on screen.)

source.title: Stride: Scale-Aware Multi-Agent Evolutionary Refinement for Infographic Generation
source.role_reason: 图1及3.1节为STRIDE整体多轮评估、路由、编辑和接受/回退流程。
source.caption:
Figure 1: Overview of STRIDE. From K initial samples, STRIDE selects a champion and refines it
for t rounds. Each round performs evolutionary refinement and agent state update through dual-route
evaluation: the verifier scores candidate images against the rubrics, while the perceptor provides vi-
sual grounding of the observed failures. The lead editor then analyzes the agent state and refinement
trajectory to route the champion to either the composer for global redraw or the retoucher for local
editing. The generated candidates are then re-evaluated, and the champion is updated only when a
candidate improves the verifier score. Repeating this process yields the final champion.

observations.evidence: The left-to-right sequence identifies initialization, evaluation, lead-editor routing, and Composer/Retoucher execution. The right-hand sequence shows champion acceptance and rollback across rounds.
observations.limitation: The connection between generated candidates, dual-route evaluation, and subsequent champion selection requires tracing several loosely connected regions.

source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of RwF. Filter localization (left): parameter-space integrated gradients rank
layers, then filters within them, and the selected set is expanded with high-IG, low-similarity filters.
Filter learning (right): the localized filters are regenerated from a filter bank by factorized matrices
with cross-task attention and assembled back into the frozen backbone.

observations.evidence: The top sequence clearly connects warm-up training, Filter Localization, Filter Learning, and the next task. Enlarged modules expose attribution, expansion, attention, and filter assembly.
observations.limitation: The learning module does not clearly distinguish how the selected and expansion sets feed its computation.

source.caption:
Figure 2. The overall inference pipeline of SegEarth-OV3. Given an input image and a list of text prompts, we leverage SAM 3’s decoupled
outputs. The pipeline involves: (1) instance aggregation to consolidate sparse object queries; (2) dual-head mask fusion to combine the
fine-grained instance details with the global coverage of the semantic head; and (3) presence-guided filtering (using the presence score) to
suppress false positives from absent categories. denotes the element-wise maximum operation, and denotes multiplication.

source.caption:
Figure 1. We show how the proposed concept IRP differs from
the traditional image metric visual quality. Given a sequence of
images captured under varying exposures in dynamic scenes (first
row), both IQA metric NIQE [23] and human observers favorite
either (a) or (b) as relatively good shots, but they do not neces-
sarily lead to better restored results (second row). As a compari-
son, a perceptually poor image (c) leads to the best restored image
quality. The result indicates the necessity of developing the IRP
metric which predicts if the restored image quality will be good
even before it is processed. All images are processed by the same
restoration model MPR [40] to ensure fairness.

source.caption:
Figure 1. When a 3D reconstructor is trained using only a single
viewperobject,becauseofambiguityinthe3Dshapeofanobject,
itreconstructsashape whichonly fitsthe observedview andlooks
incorrect from unobserved viewpoints (upper). By introducing a
discriminator that learns prior knowledge of correct views, the re-

source.caption:
Fig. 1. Pipelines of classical GFSS works and our Syn4Seg framework.
(a) Classical GFSS methods follow three stages: base class learning, novel
class registration, and evaluation, where novel classes rely on limited manual
annotations, resulting in low diversity and constrained performance. (b) Our
Syn4Seg framework synthesizes diverse, realistic novel class images and
pseudo labels guided by support annotations. These synthesized samples,
together with base data, are used to train a semantic segmentation model,
enabling robust recognition of both base and novel classes during evaluation.

source.caption:
Figure 2. (a) For the COCO dataset, all the images are resized such that the short edge has 800 pixels while the long edge has less than
1333 pixels. For the ImageNet dataset, all the images are resized to 224×224 to calculate the statistics. The scale of object is represented
as the square root of the area. We discuss the typical training input size for ImageNet classification and COCO detection tasks. (b) All the
scores are predicted on COCO minival dataset by the RetinaNet detector with FPN and ResNet 50 backbone, which is trained with 10%
COCO data. The score distance is the absolute difference between the predictions of the image in different sizes. The Y-axis is the average
numberofanchorsperimage. (c)Wepredictpseudo-labelontherestofCOCOtrainingdatawithaconvergedFaster-RCNNdetector(with
FPNandResNet50backbone), trainedwith10%COCOdata. Thelowaveragerecallandprecisionshowthathardpseudo-labelincurmore
noise with False Negative samples.

source.caption:
Figure 1. The framework of Class-balanced Pixel-level Self-Labeling (CPSL). The model contains a main segmentation network f and
SEG
its momentum-updated version f′ . The f′ is followed by a self-labeling head f and its momentum version f′ , which projects
SEG SEG SL SL
pixel-wise feature embedding into a class probability vector. The pixel-level self-labeling module produces soft cluster assignment P to
SL
gradually rectify soft pseudo label P . Then the segmentation loss Lt is computed between the prediction map P and the rectified
ST SEG
pseudo label Yˆt. To train the self-labeling head, we randomly sample pixels from each image, and use the memory bank M, which
contains previous batches of pixel features, to augment the current batch. Then we compute the optimal transport assignment Q over
aug
the augmented data by enforcing class balance, and use the assignment of current batch Q to compute the self-labeling loss L .

source.caption:
Figure 1: The “last-mile” problem in generative image restoration. State-of-the-art methods (Yu
et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024b; Lin et al., 2025) produce globally plausible reconstructions from
severely degraded inputs, yet localized failures persist. Despite their small spatial extent, these
failures dominate perceived quality and practical acceptability.

observations.evidence: The input-to-restoration arrows and enlarged restoration/GT comparisons clearly communicate that global improvement can leave local failures.
observations.limitation: The correspondence between the two crop comparisons and two failure labels in each row is implicit.

observations.evidence: The left-to-right sequence explicitly contrasts degraded inputs, globally restored images, and local failures beside GT references. Text, faces, furniture, and water illustrate how convincing restoration can retain localized errors.
observations.limitation: The correspondence between each colored failure label and its crop pair is implicit.

observations.evidence: The input-to-restoration sequence and enlarged comparisons with GT clearly show local failures despite improved overall images.
observations.limitation: The correspondence between each failure label and its crop pair is implicit.

observations.evidence: Four aligned example rows follow the same left-to-right sequence under clearly legible column headings.
observations.limitation: The comparison region is dense, with borders, dashed dividers, GT labels, and face icons competing for space.

observations.evidence: Four aligned example rows and prominent column headings establish a clear reading order. Arrows connect restored images to enlarged comparison regions.
observations.limitation: The tightly packed comparisons require close inspection, and yellow failure labels have weak contrast against white.

source.title: DeCo: A Multimodal Detection Framework based on Density Consensus Learning
source.role_reason: 图2覆盖多尺度编码、密度共识估计、融合检测与密度监督完整路径，正文称为DeCo overview。
source.pdf_version: ICLR 2027 frozen anonymous submission PDF; retrieved 2026-10-28 UTC
source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of DeCo. Independent backbones extract multimodal, multiscale features, which
are projected into a shared density space to estimate modality reliability and construct density con-
sensus. The resulting consensus guides multiscale feature fusion for detection and is simultaneously
decoded into a density map for density supervision.

observations.evidence: The four stages communicate optical/SAR feature extraction, density consensus, multiscale fusion, and detection plus density outputs.
observations.limitation: Connections between stages II, III, and IV rely on matching symbols rather than explicit routes; the sequential arrows between losses are ambiguous.

observations.evidence: The four named stages establish optical/SAR inputs, density consensus estimation, multiscale fusion, and detection/density outputs. The reliability maps and weighted-consensus equation explain the central fusion mechanism.
observations.limitation: Connections between stages II, III, and IV rely partly on repeated symbols rather than explicit routing.

observations.evidence: The optical and SAR streams visibly converge through a shared projector and consensus gating, followed by fusion and detection/density outputs.
observations.limitation: Connections between stages rely on matching symbols rather than explicit routing. The consensus-feature branch appears before Softmax even though its formula uses the resulting reliability weights.

observations.evidence: Numbered stage headings and shaded groups establish a clear hierarchy, with parallel modality streams across the top.
observations.limitation: The narrow fusion strip compresses several equations and explanations, while the supervision region requires close reading of small text.

observations.evidence: Numbered stage headings, dashed boundaries, and tinted groups establish a clear overall hierarchy. Parallel encoder rows make the two input streams easy to compare.
observations.limitation: The narrow fusion band compresses several equations and explanatory boxes, while the supervision region requires close reading of small text.

observations.evidence: Numbered stage headings, paired encoder rows, and separate detection and density panels establish a clear hierarchy. The crops make the detailed formulas inspectable.
observations.limitation: The narrow fusion strip and compact loss equations require more reading effort than the larger encoder blocks.

observations.evidence: Green optical and blue SAR features remain traceable through the encoders, projector outputs, and reliability maps.
observations.limitation: The SAR encoder is also titled 'Optical density encoder,' and the fusion-cell input depicts both modality features with a green stack, weakening the established encoding.

observations.evidence: Green optical features and blue SAR features recur through extraction, projection, and reliability estimation. Matching encoder shapes reinforce parallel processing.
observations.limitation: The SAR branch is also labeled 'Optical density encoder,' and the stage III input stack uses green for both feature labels, weakening modality traceability.

observations.evidence: Green optical features and blue SAR features recur through extraction, projection, and the mixed-color fused tensors.
observations.limitation: The SAR encoder is also titled 'Optical density encoder.' The fusion-cell input depicts both modality features with a green tensor, weakening the established color distinction.

observations.evidence: Muted green and blue panels, repeated rounded boxes, and aligned modality streams create a coherent composition.
observations.limitation: The dense middle strip and crowded lower-right formulas create uneven visual weight relative to the more spacious upper-right region.

observations.evidence: Muted green and blue fills, repeated rounded boxes, and consistent black outlines visually unify the architecture. Red text selectively emphasizes the density consensus feature.
observations.limitation: The dense middle equation strip and uneven whitespace across the upper section slightly disrupt visual balance.

observations.evidence: Muted green and blue panels, repeated rounded boxes, and aligned encoder rows give the composition visual coherence.
observations.limitation: Nested dashed boundaries, tensor grids, and tightly packed equations make the middle and lower regions visually busier than the upper region.

observations.evidence: Complementary reliability grids and mixed-color fused feature stacks help illustrate modality combination; the trust and enhancement callouts interpret the fusion computation.
observations.limitation: Most relationships use conventional module boxes, and the reliability grids lack a concrete example showing how trust changes across image regions.

observations.evidence: Complementary colored reliability grids and mixed-color output stacks help visualize modality weighting and fusion. The 'which modality to trust' and 'where to enhance or suppress' annotations translate equations into functional ideas.
observations.limitation: Much of the explanation still uses conventional module boxes and feature stacks; the grids do not demonstrate weighting on a concrete scene.

observations.evidence: Complementary reliability grids and mixed-color feature tensors help explain spatially varying modality contributions. The 'which modality to trust' and 'where to enhance or suppress' labels interpret the fusion computation.
observations.limitation: Most operations remain conventional boxes and equations; the example imagery does not illustrate a concrete change caused by consensus weighting.

observations.evidence: Paired optical/SAR imagery, spatial reliability maps, density-conditioned fusion equations, and separate detection and density outputs express the framework's distinctive operations.
observations.limitation: Some internal operations, including the shared projector and context aggregation, remain abstract labeled modules.

observations.evidence: Paired optical/SAR imagery, spatial reliability maps, density-guided modulation, and separate detection and density outputs express this architecture's distinctive relationships. The supervision blocks further specify box-aware mass assignment, structural consistency, and count constraints.
observations.limitation: The correspondence between the scene examples, reliability grids, and resulting density maps is not explicitly illustrated.

observations.evidence: Paired optical/SAR imagery, spatial reliability maps, consensus-guided multiscale fusion, and separate detection and density supervision express a distinctive architecture.
observations.limitation: Individual backbone and decoder blocks remain abstract, although their relationships are tailored to this framework.

Figure 1: Target-support use in FT-FSOD (Yu et al., 2026) and PULSE. (a) FT-FSOD uses support
annotations for target-domain fine-tuning and subsequently scores query predictions without explicitly
consulting the support examples. (b) PULSE retains cached support evidence and uses SSCA to
refine classification scores according to support–query agreement. Box tags denote predicted classes,
and bar lengths illustrate schematic confidence. The dashed candidate illustrates score suppression at
the same location. Test images from DeepFish (Fu et al., 2024) are used for illustration; the support
examples, bounding boxes, and score changes are schematic.

source.caption:
Figure 5. The proposed framework of our DADA. It includes a source branch and a target branch, both of which have an LR-HR-LR
reconstruction structure. In their up-sampling networks, a Domain-Invariant Attention (DIA) module provides component attentive masks
by a pre-trained CDC model. For InterAA, two LR images from different domains are fed into the up-sampling network for adversarial
adaptation in one branch. For IntraAA, one LR image is respectively fed into up-sampling networks in source and target branches for the
adversarial adaptation. For testing, the trained up-sampling network in target branch is utilized for inference.

source.caption:
Fig. 2. The overview of the proposed PWOOD framework. Orientation Learning and Scale Learning modules enables the Orientation-and-Scale-aware Student
to learn both scale and orientation information from weakly annotated data, as well as Class-Agnostic Pseudo-Label Filtering mechanism enhances pseudo-label
quality by leveraging dynamic thresholds.

observations.evidence: The student–teacher split, EMA arrow, and labeled scale, orientation, and pseudo-label filtering modules establish the main training process.
observations.limitation: Merged prediction connectors and unlabeled dot grids make the precise exchanges between modules harder to interpret.

observations.evidence: Labeled student and teacher branches, an EMA connection, and separate scale, orientation, and filtering modules communicate the main training framework.
observations.limitation: The prediction grids lack explicit labels, and the connections between filtering, threshold selection, and student supervision require interpretation.

observations.evidence: The student and teacher branches, EMA connection, and named learning modules establish the main training process.
observations.limitation: The shared prediction connectors and looping threshold path leave some module inputs and filtering relationships unclear.

observations.limitation: The dense right side and long threshold feedback connector complicate the reading sequence. Small loss labels require the detail views.

observations.limitation: The dense right side and long threshold feedback connector complicate the reading sequence; small scale-learning annotations require the crops.

observations.evidence: Inputs sit on the left, learning modules on the right, and a dashed divider separates student and teacher.
observations.limitation: Dense equations, branching connectors, and the irregular filtering enclosure make the right-hand reading sequence effortful.

observations.evidence: Red and blue consistently distinguish augmented and original views, while teal tracks unlabeled inputs and the teacher branch.
observations.limitation: The dot-grid shading lacks an explicit key, and the joined red–blue connectors obscure which predictions feed each learning module.

observations.evidence: Red and blue distinguish augmented and original predictions, teal tracks unlabeled inputs, and purple consistently marks filtering operations.

source.caption:
Figure 3: ARROW architecture. The multi-view encoder E tokenizes each frame independently
and employs global attention to produce a shared global context F together with an ID token h for
i
each frame. The query encoder combines a source-centered RGB crop, the Fourier-encoded (u, v)
coordinate, and the ID tokens of the queried source, target, and reference view frames into a latent
query token z . Each latent query token independently cross-attends to the global context, so a single
q
encoding serves arbitrarily many queries and yields a consistent 4D representation of the scene.

source.caption: Figure 2: Overview of GenRevisit. Panel (a) presents the overall workflow. At each decision step, the multimodal planner selects the next action based on the decision context and, when editing, jointly selects a source image as the continuation state and a corresponding edit specification. The resulting image is verified and recorded in the interaction history to inform subsequent decisions, while submission returns the historical GM-best image. Panel (b) illustrates an editing example. The planner selects I₁, which is neither the latest candidate I₂ nor the GM-best candidate I₀, and corrects the backpack count while preserving the other constraints. The resulting candidate I₃ passes all constraint-level checks and becomes the new GM-best image.

source.caption:
Figure 1. Comparing generative open-ended object detection with
other open-set object detection tasks. Open-vocabulary object de-
tection and phrase grounding typically require predefined cate-
gories or phrases in text prompts to align with image regions. In
contrast, our introduced generative open-ended object detection is
a more general and practical setting where categorical information
is not explicitly defined. Such a setting is especially meaningful
for scenarios where users lack precise knowledge of object cate-
gories during inference.

observations.evidence: Three labeled rows contrast predefined categories, caption phrases, and generated object descriptions using the same image. Their outputs make the different vocabulary constraints visible.
observations.limitation: The motivation for open-ended generation is implied by the comparison rather than explicitly stated.

source.title: SimT: Handling Open-set Noise for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation
source.role_reason: 图2为完整域适应训练框架，覆盖输入、分割网、噪声转换、监督校正及三个正则化支路。
source.caption:
Figure 2. The proposed domain adaption framework contains a segmentation net and a SimT. Target images are passed through the
segmentation net f(·) to perform semantic segmentation, and supervision signals are corrected by the learnable SimT. SimT is estimated
w
through the proposed (a) volume regularization, (b) anchor guidance and (c) convex guarantee.

source.caption:
Figure 4. Native resolution example. Methods like DUSt3R require centered principal point and would thus downscale the image to its
training resolution, leading to blurry prediction (top). With camera intrinsics input, we can process any crop in the image leading to native
resolution prediction (bottom row), for example by dividing the image into 4 crops, that are independently process as the first input image,
while the second input image of the network is set to the downscaled image.

observed only after execution, while decisions remain restricted to the available action space. Pre-

source.title: PassionSR: Post-Training Quantization with Adaptive Scale in One-Step Diffusion based Image Super-Resolution
source.role_reason: 图4 Overview完整串联UNet–VAE简化、LBQ/LET可学习量化参数和分布量化校准三步骤；第3节逐项对应，属于全方法流程。
source.caption:
Figure 4. Overview of our PassionSR. Step 1: we simplify OSEDiff [42] by removing DAPE and CLIP Encoder, obtaining PassionSR-
FP. Step 2: the quantizer we use has two key trainable parts, consisting of the Learnable Boundary Quantizer and Learnable Equivalent
Transformation. Step 3: we design a distributed calibration strategy and special loss function to accelerate convergence of calibration.

source.role_reason: 首图用三个标注任务展示单图重建、跨实例稠密对应及纹理迁移的应用关系；引言第2页解释共同形状表示如何支撑后两项用途。按应用场景收录，不因渲染质量评选。
source.caption:
Figure 1. Given an unpaired image collection (with known camera poses) of an object category at training time, our approach learns to: (a)
reconstruct the underlying 3D given only a single image at test time, and (b) model dense 3D correspondences across category instances.
The learned correspondence field is articulation-aware, topologically-aware and inherently captures structural properties of the category,
enabling the task of unsupervised texture transfer. Videos and code at https://shivamduggal4.github.io/tars-3D/

els through a transformer network. This enriched understanding of

source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of PreActIR. The world model predicts action consequences before execution,
while the predict–act–verify controller executes and verifies the selected action with commit or
rollback. A tool-evolution loop performs candidate-frontier audit and targeted tool adaptation.

observations.limitation: The connection between verified outcomes and the lower tool-evolution loop is not explicitly traced.

Figure 2. Framework overview. Best viewed in color. We develop the high-level feature alignment into separate task spaces, by applying
the proposed Task-specific Inconsistency Alignment module to both the classification (green part) and localization (blue part) branches
of the baseline detector (gray part). In each branch, the behavioral inconsistency of multiple auxiliary predictors is optimized via the
corresponding inconsistency-aware loss, for essentially bridging the category-wise or boundary-wise margins between domains.

source.title: LAB-Det: Language as a Domain-Invariant Bridge for Training-Free One-Shot Domain Generalization in Object Detection
source.role_reason: 图1及引言解释专域单样本稀缺、歧义与微调过拟合，概念对比语言域桥接路径。
source.caption:
Figure 1. Challenge and conceptual comparison of training-free 1-
shot domain generalization for object detection. (a) In specialized
domains (e.g., underwater or industrial), data can be very scarce
(e.g., only one labeled exemplar per class) and object boundaries
are ambiguous, making general-domain detectors fail under severe
domain gaps. (b) Training-based approaches rely on fine-tuning
with gradient updates, which incur extra cost, overfit under 1-shot
supervision, and remain unstable in high-IB domains. In contrast,
LAB-Det leverages language as a domain-invariant bridge: sup-
port exemplars are re-expressed as descriptive text and injected
into frozen vision–language models, enabling training-free, inter-
pretable, and robust target-domain detection.

source.caption:
Figure 1. Training process for OVD using frozen CLIP. (a) Com-
monly used training process, (b) Our training process.

source.title: Efficient Test-time Adaptive Object Detection via Sensitivity-Guided Pruning
source.role_reason: 引言图1以连续变化的道路天气和在线适应示意应用问题，说明在算力受限场景中选择不变通道的动机。
source.caption:
Figure 1. We consider continual test-time adaptive object detec-
tion, which adapts a source detector to changing environments
during inference. By focusing adaptation efforts on invariant
parts while pruning sensitive parts, we improve computational ef-
ficiency, which is crucial for resource-constrained scenarios like
autonomous driving or UAV.

source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of the proposed DCHA framework. (a) DCHA constructs category-specific
LoRA by composing vectors from a shared bank and averages the resulting category updates to form
the task-level adaptation for the VLF layers. (b) LCAR transforms category-specific routing logits
into sparse composition weights using a learnable sparsity coefficient, enabling category-dependent
vector selection. (c) HDC preserves historical adaptation knowledge by constraining deviations at
the bank-vector, category-update, and task-update levels.

source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of our framework. From a single image, scene initialization (Stage 1), environ-
ment construction (Stage 2), and scene refinement (Stage 3) build a complete 3D scene. In Stage 1,
the geometry-aware layout predictor regresses per-object R, T , S, and floor rotation F .

source.caption: Figure 1: Motivation of AKI. (a) Under fixed model capacity, inherited constraints can restrict the representation reorganization required by current supervision, increasing old–new distribution overlap. (b) Cross-step optimization analysis shows that adjacent incremental objectives generally correspond to different stationary states, θ*_(t−1) ≠ θ*_t, while inheritance constraints can restrict current-task-aligned adaptation. (c) Empirical analysis reveals cross-level coupling among response, feature, and distribution variations, motivating coordinated knowledge reorganization across three levels.

source.caption: Figure 1. Typical diffusion processes. (a) Standard diffusion maps high-quality images to Gaussian noise domain. (b) Mean-reverting diffusion drives terminal state toward a low-quality domain with stationary noise. (c) Diffusion bridge establishes direct probabilistic transitions between known distributions. All inject noise globally, disrupting overall structures and constraining transitions. (d) In contrast, our RDBM selectively reconstructs degraded regions (e.g., the doll) while preserving intact areas (e.g., the background).

source.caption:
Figure 2. Overall architecture of MFuser. MFuser takes inputs through both VFM and VLM visual encoders. Features from each encoder
layer are concatenated and refined in MVFuser, which captures sequential and spatial dependencies in parallel. The refined features are
then added back to the original features and passed to the next layer. MTEnhancer strengthens text embeddings of each class by integrating
visualfeaturesthroughahybridattention-Mambamechanism. TheenhancedtextembeddingsserveasobjectqueriesfortheMask2Former
decoder, alongside multi-scale visual features. During training, only MVFusers, MTEnhancers, and the segmentation decoder are trainable
while the VFM and VLM remain frozen, preserving their generalization ability and enabling efficient training. Note that skip connections
between each block of MTEnhancer are omitted for clarity.

source.title: GATOR: Generative and Agentic 3D Object Reconstruction from Casual Images
source.role_reason: 图2与方法节展示生成重建和智能体细化的完整两阶段体系。
source.caption:
Fig. 2: GATOR architecture. (A) Pose-aware generative reconstruction. Following TRELLIS.2 (Xiang
et al., 2026), GATOR uses conditional flows for sparse structure, geometry, and appearance. RGB images and
depth-derived pointmaps retain scene context, while masks identify the target. Tokens from all three modalities
share a patch grid with common 2D position and Plücker-ray encodings. A local mixer exchanges information
at each patch within a view (Secs. 3.2 and 3.3). Cross-view attention and SigLIP2 object-name conditioning
guide structure generation. At its active coordinates, projected DINOv3 and NAF-upsampled features from
target-masked images are averaged across valid views and injected into every geometry and appearance de-
noising block. Global image tokens and T5Gemma2-encoded captions supply cross-attention. Shape latents
condition PBR material generation (Sec. 3.4). ❄ denotes frozen encoders. (B) Agentic refinement. Initialized
with the complete, scene-aligned asset, an agent uses input images and structural priors to complete parts, re-
pair topology, and refine texture coordinates and materials. Its edit-render-review loop compares original and
candidate renders under matched cameras and lighting to retain or revert local edits. Within the time budget, it
selects the best inspected asset while preserving reliable regions and scene-relative placement (Sec. 3.5).

source.role_reason: 图2为PCAsplat核心计算路径，完整呈现高斯邻域、可微PCA、谱约束、法线对齐到表面对齐高斯。

source.caption:
Figure 2: Overview of PCAsplat. We regularize Gaussian neighborhoods directly in scene space.
For each Gaussian, we estimate a local neighborhood and compute differentiable PCA statistics
that capture the underlying tangent structure. We then regularize the local eigenspectrum to reduce
neighborhood thickness and promote isotropic tangent-plane coverage. We also align Gaussian
normals with PCA-derived normals, encouraging surface-aligned and well-localized splats. Our
formulation is lightweight, differentiable, and directly compatible with existing splatting pipelines.

source.caption:
Figure 2. The pipeline of our proposed DenSe Learning (DSL) based SSOD method. The training data contain both labeled and unlabeled
images. During each training iteration, a teacher model is employed to produce pseudo-labels for weakly augmented unlabeled images.
In anchor-free based detectors like FCOS [44], each spatial location of the dense predictions will be assigned with one label, and the
model performance is sensitive to noisy pseudo-labels. To alleviate this problem, an Adaptive Filtering strategy is proposed to split the
pseudo-labels into three types, including background, foreground and ignorable regions. Moreover, there exist some false positive cases,
which have higher scores but are obviously wrong predictions. Thus, a MetaNet is proposed to refine these cases. To improve the model
generalization capability, unlabeled images are patch-shuffled and consistency regularizations are applied on these images with different
scales. For improving the stability and quality of pseudo-labels, the teacher model is updated by the student models via aggregation, called
Aggregated Teacher. After obtaining the fine-grained pixel-wise pseudo-labels, the detector can be optimized by the final loss, which is the
sum of L ,L and L .

source.caption: Figure 2: SCLE only modifies the pre-decoder selection stage of the language-guided detector. Left: detection pipeline, where SCLE-driven query selection replaces text-score ranking before the HED decoder. Upper right: class-wise foreground prototypes and one shared background prototype, updated by exponential moving average from labeled support samples. Lower right: the prototype bank produces a class-agnostic evidence map. Candidates are scored using interior purity P_i, ring evidence R_i, and contrast C_i. A quota divides the Top-900 budget into semantic, local-evidence and joint channels. Only the indices fed into the decoder are changed.

source.caption:
Figure 2: Persistent support evidence and SSCA-centered calibration in PULSE. In Stage I, HED
is fine-tuned on the target support set, and the resulting encoder snapshot is frozen to construct the
evidence bank E. In Stage II, the query detector is initialized with the Stage I weights and produces
query features Q, base class logits S, and predicted boxes B. SSCA matches Q with the cached
evidence E to obtain support agreement s and refines the base logits as S′ = S + G ⊙ ∆, while the
box coordinates bypass score calibration and remain unchanged. The evidence bank remains fixed
throughout Stage II training and inference. Flames indicate trainable parameters during training,
whereas snowflakes indicate frozen modules or fixed evidence. All model parameters are fixed during
inference. Test images from the DeepFish dataset (Fu et al., 2024) are adopted for illustration and do
not correspond to the sampled adaptation episode; the displayed output box is schematic rather than
an actual model prediction.

observations.evidence: Support examples feed a frozen evidence bank, while query features and base logits feed support matching and score calibration before decoding.

tation to underwater scenarios in terms of (a) datasets and (b-c)

source.caption:
Figure 2. The entire architecture of our method. We compare the adjusted embeddings, produced by the DINOv2 model, of the positive
and negative support images, with the relevant masks extracted using the SAM model to provide an initial estimate of our segmentation
BBox. We again use DINOv2 for generating pixel-precise heatmaps which provide another estimate for the segmentation. We combine
both these estimates using a binarized overlap to get the final segmentation mask.

source.title: Decoupling Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation
source.role_reason: 引言与图1对比像素级和片段级零样本分类，图中同时展示像素方法失败与分组解耦思路；用于引出建模限制。
source.caption:
Figure 1. ZS3 aims to train a model merely on seen classes and
generalize it to classes that have not been seen in the training (un-
seen classes). Existing methods formulate it as a pixel-level zero-
shot classification problem (b), and use semantic features from a
language model to transfer the knowledge from seen classes to
unseen ones. In contrast, as in (c), we decouple ZS3 into two
sub-tasks: 1) A class-agnostic grouping and 2) A segment-level
zero-shot classification, which enables us to take full advantage of
the pre-trained vision-language model.

source.title: Carve3D: Improving Multi-view Reconstruction Consistency for Diffusion Models with RL Finetuning
source.role_reason: 图2明确为Carve3D整体框架，包含文本条件去噪、NeRF重建与渲染、MRC奖励和梯度更新。
source.caption:
Figure 2. Overview of Carve3D. Given a prompt sampled from our curated prompt set and a initial noisy image, we iteratively denoise
the image using the UNet. The final, clean image contains four multi-view images tiled in a 2-by-2 grid. MRC reward is computed by
comparing (a) the generated multi-view images with (c) the corresponding multi-view images rendered at the same camera viewpoints
from (b) the reconstructed NeRF. Then, we train the model with policy gradient loss function, where the loss is derived from the reward
and log probabilities of the UNet’s predictions, accumulated over all denoising timesteps. By using only a set of training text prompts, our
RLFT algorithm finetunes the diffusion model by evaluating its own generated outputs, without relying on ground truth multi-view images.

Figure 1. Illustration of Novel Class Discovery in Semantic Seg-
mentation(NCDSS).Givenalabeledset(person,horse,motorbike
and car) and a class disjoint unlabeled set (bike and boat), NCDSS
aims at leveraging all the data to segment novel images.

source.caption:
Figure 1: (a) Overall pipeline of our any-depth object detection network, following the standard
backbone–neck–head design common to modern detectors such as RT-DETR and YOLO, operating
on multi-scale features. Each stage in both the backbone and neck is divided into an essential path
(solid blocks) and a skippable refinement path (dashed blocks). At inference time, any combination
of essential and full paths across stages yields a valid sub-network, enabling a continuous range of
accuracy–efficiency trade-offs from a single set of weights. (b) A residual-block stage, as used in
RT-DETR. (c) A CSP-style stage, as used in the YOLO family. In both stage types, the essential and
full paths are jointly trained via self-distillation to produce aligned feature representations at each
stage boundary, so that downstream stages can process the output of either path reliably.

source.title: SplatSuRe: Selective Super-Resolution for Multi-view Consistent 3D Gaussian Splatting
source.role_reason: 图2及方法部分给出LR三维模型、区域选择、SR模型与HR三维模型及两种损失的整体训练关系；主要任务为场景三维重建。
source.caption:
Figure 2. Overview of our SplatSuRe framework. A high-resolution (HR) 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model is trained using low-
resolution (LR) and super-resolution (SR) inputs. We first train a 3DGS model on LR inputs to identify undersampled regions and render
per-view weight maps that indicate where SR is needed. During training of the HR 3DGS model, the images produced by the frozen
single-image super-resolution (SISR) model are spatially weighted by these maps to form the SR loss L . A complementary LR loss
SR
L compares the downsampled HR render against the original LR ground truth to provide consistent supervision across the entire image.
LR

source.caption:
Figure 1. Different paradigms of isotropic reconstruction from
anisotropic datasets. Existing approaches typically extract vol-
ume features from abundant xy-plane images. After stacking
anisotropic slices along the z-axis (top), they: (a) Video inter-
polation along the z-axis: models are trained along the x or y
direction, where adjacent frames are input to synthesize the inter-
mediate frame; during inference, the trained model is repurposed
to interpolate along the z-axis, generating intermediate slices cor-
responding to continuous temporal coordinates (τ ∈ [0, 1]). (b)
Image super-resolution on xz/yz planes: Since the xy-plane im-
ages are of much higher resolution, a low-resolution counterpart
can be generated either by manual downsampling [21] or by learn-
ing a degradation model [6], forming paired HR–LR supervision
for training; during inference, the resulting super-resolution model
is then applied along the z-axis to enhance xz/yz slices. Both
paradigms implicitly assume spatial isotropy. In contrast, our
method directly performs inference in continuous 3D space, with-
out relying on such isotropic assumptions.

source.role_reason: 图2展示完整DASR训练与两类域距离监督路径。
source.caption:
Figure 2: Illustration of our DASR framework. DASR firstly trains a down-sampling network (DSN) which aims to generate
LR images y g in the real LR domain y r from HR images xr : y g = DS N (xr ). Then, DASR take the domain-gap between
generated LR images y g and real-world LR images y r into consideration, utilize the generated LR-HR pairs {y g , xr }, domain
distance maps w and real-world LR images y r to train super-resolution network (SRN).

source.title: Decoupling Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation
source.role_reason: 正文图2明确为完整ZegFormer流程，包含查询、图像与文本编码、掩码与语义投影以及训练和推理路径。
source.caption:
Figure 2. The pipeline of our proposed ZegFormer for zero-shot semantic segmentation. We first feed N queries and feature maps to a
transformer decoder to generate N segment embeddings. We then feed each segment embedding to a mask projection layer and a semantic
projection layer to obtain a mask embedding and a semantic embedding. Mask embedding is multiplied with the output of pixel decoder
to generate a class-agnostic binary mask, while The semantic embedding is classified by the text embeddings. The text embeddings are
generated by putting the class names into a prompt template and then feeding them to a text encoder of a vision-language model. During
training, only the seen classes are used to train the segment-level classification head. During inference, both the text embeddings of seen
and unseen classes are used for segment-level classification. We can obtain two segment-level classification scores with semantic segment
embeddings and image embeddings. Finally, we fuse the these two classification scores as our final class prediction of segments.

source.caption:
Figure 2. Training pipeline of NAS3R. Subscripts “C ” and “T ” denote context and target views, respectively. Unconstrained images are
patchified into visual tokens and concatenated with a learnable camera token for camera prediction. A masked decoder regulates cross-view
interactions and prevents target-to-context leakage. Refined context tokens are then processed by the Gaussian head to predict Gaussian
parameters, while a depth head estimates depth maps that are lifted into 3D Gaussian centers using the predicted context poses. The
predicted target poses are finally used to render novel views, providing photometric supervision for end-to-end training.

source.title: EW-DETR: Evolving World Object Detection via Incremental Low-Rank DEtection TRansformer
source.role_reason: 图3展示完整的EW-DETR主干、LoRA、查询标准化、未知类别混合及检测输出；图2含概念与简略流程，图3为正文完整框架。
source.caption:
Figure 3. EW-DETR framework for Evolving-World Object Detection. An input image is processed by a frozen backbone and
transformer encoder–decoder equipped with aggregate (cid:0) ∆Wt−1 (cid:1) and task-specific (cid:0) ∆Wt (cid:1) LoRA adapters, yielding class-agnostic
agg task
query features. These queries are reparameterised by the Query-Norm Objectness Adapter and passed through a classification head and
an objectness head, whose outputs are combined by Entropy-aware Unknown Mixing module to produce calibrated class scores, while a
localisation head predicts bounding boxes to form final detections across tasks1 .

source.caption:
Figure 5. Illustration of the proposed plane splatting function.
Naive Gaussian Splatting can not effectively approximate the
boundary of our rectangular plane primitive (shown in black
dashed border). In contrast, our proposed plane splatting function
can approximate the boundary of the rectangle as the number of
iterations increases, allowing our 3D planar primitives to better fit
the surface of the scene.

source.caption:
Figure 3. Illustration of our proposed PlanarSplatting. Given a set of posed multi-view images of indoor scenes, our method renders
depth and normal maps from 3D plane primitives. Then, with the supervision of monocular cues, these 3D plane primitives are gradually
optimized to recover the scene geometry and finally merged to get the planar reconstruction result.

Figure 1. Illustration of our proposed training framework for con-
tinual semantic segmentation to avoid catastrophic forgetting. We
design two mechanisms in our method, representation compensa-
tion (RC) module and pooled cube distillation (PCD).

source.caption:
Figure 1: BodyBound in simulation. (a) Task schematics show six families and their intervened
body parameters. (b) Paired comparisons change the physical body with its matching description,
or the description alone. (c) Policies act from public observations, goals, and body descriptions;
fresh observations close the loop, while an independent checker evaluates measured traces. HPT
and Diffusion Policy use RGB, not depth. (d) Familiar starts, expert executions, and unchanged-
command replay separate task competence, attainability, and shared solutions. Scene geometry
stays fixed within each pair.

source.title: SAGE: Style-Adaptive Generalization for Privacy-Constrained Semantic Segmentation Across Domains
source.role_reason: 引言以图1对比标准DGSS、隐私禁止调参及固定风格提示失败，明确问题约束；不是仅报告准确率的结果图。
source.caption:
Figure 1. Overview of domain generalization settings under privacy constraints. (a) Standard DGSS requires backbone tuning. (b) Style-
fixed prompting is ineffective on unseen domains. (c) SAGE inference overcomes privacy limitations.

observations.evidence: The three panels contrast standard DGSS, a privacy limitation with a bad segmentation result, and SAGE inference with a good result. Frozen-model icons and the crossed-out tuning arrow make the constraint explicit.
observations.limitation: The source–prompt combination and its connection to domain shift are less clearly explained.

observations.evidence: The three panels explicitly contrast standard DGSS, a privacy-related failure, and SAGE inference using good/bad segmentation outputs and check/cross markers.
observations.limitation: The connection between the fixed-style prompt, domain shift, and failure is less explicit than the overall contrast.

source.caption:
Figure 3. This diagram illustrates our multimodal super-resolution pipeline. Starting with a low-resolution (LR) image, we extract modalities
like depth and semantic segmentation maps. These modalities are encoded into tokens and transformed into multimodal latent tokens (m).
Our diffusion model uses these tokens and the LR input to generate a high-resolution (SR) output. A multimodal classifier-free guidance
(m-cfg) refines the SR image for enhanced quality.

source.caption: Figure 2. A schematic of Residual Diffusion Bridge Models. RDBM utilizes a diffusion process guided by Doob’s h-transform towards an endpoint xT = µ free from stationary noise λϵ. Modulated by the residual component π = x0 − xT , the noise perturbation is selectively imposed on different regions with diverse degradation levels, thereby constructing probabilistic paths. Besides, it learns to reverse the process by matching the residual bridge score functions, facilitating an adaptive inversion from xT ∼ pprior(x) to x0 ∼ pdata(x).

source.caption:
Figure 1: Feed-forward 3D foundation models fail on transparent objects in two opposite directions.
(a) L1 depth error for a transparent object under zero-shot prediction, LoRA, and Ours. The zero-
shot prediction is dominated by overestimation associated with background leakage. LoRA reduces
the error, but underestimation around the concave interior remains, whereas our method corrects both
error directions. (b) The two error directions differ in reference availability. Background leakage
can be related to an observable background surface, whereas a filled-in concavity has no analogous
geometric reference for recovering the missing depth.

source.caption:
Figure 1: Overview: Existing 3D representations discretize
the output space differently: (a) spatially in voxel represen-
tations, (b) in terms of predicted points, and (c) in terms of
vertices for mesh representations. In contrast, (d) we pro-
pose to consider the continuous decision boundary of a clas-
sifier f (e.g., a deep neural network) as a 3D surface which
θ
allows to extract 3D meshes at any resolution.

source.caption:
Figure 2. E-RayZer Model & Training. E-RayZer first predicts camera poses and intrinsics for all images. Then it follows RayZer [25] to
split images into two sets. E-RayZer predicts explicit 3D Gaussians as scene representation from the reference views (I ), and renders the
ref
scene using self-predicted target-view (I ) cameras. Finally, E-RayZer is trained with self-supervised photometric losses on target views.

source.title: CAT: Exploiting Inter-Class Dynamics for Domain Adaptive Object Detection
source.role_reason: 图2(a)包含完整师生网络、类间关系估计、增强及损失，(b)说明增强，保留全部子图。
source.caption:
Figure 2. (a) Class-Aware Teacher (CAT) consists of: a student-teacher network; Inter-Class Relation module (ICRm), which estimates
inter-class biases; Class-Relation Augmentation, which augments images to reduce the inter-class biases by mixing the cropped instances of
related classes; and Inter-Class Loss, which emphasises the loss on highly misclassified minority classes. (b) Class-Relation Augmentation
demonstrated on majority (Car) and minority (Bus) classes.

Figure2: MultiresolutionIsoSurfaceExtraction: Wefirst
mark all points at a given resolution which have already
been evaluated as either occupied (red circles) or unoccu-
pied (cyan diamonds). We then determine all voxels that
have both occupied and unoccupied corners and mark them
as active (light red) and subdivide them into 8 subvoxels
each. Next, we evaluate all new grid points (empty circles)
that have been introduced by the subdivision. The previous
two steps are repeated until the desired output resolution is
reached. Finally we extract the mesh using the marching
cubes algorithm [44], simplify and refine the output mesh
using first and second order gradient information.

source.title: Efficient Test-time Adaptive Object Detection via Sensitivity-Guided Pruning

source.caption:
Figure 4. Overview of our method. Motivated by the observation that certain feature channels learned from the source domain negatively
impact cross-domain performance, we propose suppressing and pruning sensitive channels while adapting invariant ones. We introduce
sensitivity-guided channel pruning, which quantifies the importance of each feature channel based on its image-level and instance-level
sensitivity to domain discrepancies. We then apply a weighted sparsity loss to the learnable parameters, promoting the pruning of channels
with higher sensitivity based on the predefined threshold and ratio. To prevent the loss of potentially useful channels from early pruning,
we introduce a stochastic channel reactivation mechanism.

Figure 2. Effects of Noise on Fidelity and Controllability. Based on pretrained Qwen-Image, (a) shows the denoising results of ground-
truth (GT) under the same prompt and different levels of noise. (b) adopts low noise level and different prompts (with Chinese annotation).
(c) studies the effects of noise on LQ with the same prompt. High-noise inputs improve perceptual quality and controllability but reduce
fidelity, whereas low-noise inputs preserve original details yet fail to deliver enhanced super-resolution effects.

observations.evidence: The three panels contrast denoising outcomes under different noise levels, prompt specificity, and input quality. Enlarged sign crops reveal altered characters, preserved text, and residual blur.
observations.limitation: Panel takeaways are unstated, and the single arrows leave the mapping of conditions to paired outputs partly implicit.

observations.evidence: The three comparisons show how noise level and prompt detail affect building appearance and sign-character preservation during denoising.
observations.limitation: Output conditions are implied by vertical placement; the intended takeaway of each panel lacks an explicit label.

observations.evidence: The building examples contrast denoising outcomes under different noise levels and generic versus character-specific prompts. Enlarged text regions expose missing, distorted, or restored characters.
observations.limitation: The intended takeaway is unstated, and single arrows leave the mapping between conditions and paired outputs partly implicit.

observations.evidence: Rounded containers separate panels (a)–(c), each with an input on the left and stacked outputs on the right. Main labels and prompt text are legible across the supplied views.
